title: Vacuum Measurement: Pirani, Penning and Capacitance Manometer Explained
text:
Pressure Measurement

 Vacuum Measurement: Pirani, Penning and Capacitance Manometer Explained

 No single vacuum gauge covers the full pressure range from atmospheric down to ultra-high vacuum. Each technology works within a specific pressure range and uses a different physical principle to infer pressure.

 Pirani, Penning and capacitance manometer gauges together cover the range from roughing vacuum down to high vacuum, and each has distinct accuracy, gas-type sensitivity, and application characteristics.

 
 Pirani Gauge 
 Penning Gauge 
 Capacitance Manometer 
 Vacuum Range 
 Thermal Conductivity 
 




 Choosing the wrong vacuum gauge gives either no reading or a wildly inaccurate one. Understanding each gauge type and its pressure range is essential before specifying a vacuum system.


 
 Hello everyone, today we are going to learn about vacuum measurement using the Pirani gauge, the Penning gauge, and the capacitance manometer.


 We will cover the working principle of each type, the pressure range each covers, how gas type affects the reading, and a comparison table to help you select the right gauge for your application.


 
 
 
 Vacuum Measurement: Three Gauge Types and Their Pressure Ranges


 
 
 Pirani Gauge

 Thermal conductivity gauge. Measures heat loss from a heated filament to surrounding gas molecules. Works from 1 atm down to 10-3 mbar (1000 Pa to 0.1 Pa).

 Gas-type dependent. Used for roughing and medium vacuum monitoring.

 

 
 Penning Gauge

 Cold cathode ionisation gauge. Measures ion current produced by electron bombardment of gas molecules. Works from 10-2 to 10-7 mbar.

 Gas-type dependent. Used for high vacuum monitoring and interlock systems.

 

 
 Capacitance Manometer

 Mechanical diaphragm gauge. Measures physical deflection of a thin metal diaphragm against a reference vacuum. Works from atmosphere down to 10-4 mbar.

 Gas-type independent. The most accurate of the three types.

 Pirani Gauge Working Principle


 The Pirani gauge uses the thermal conductivity of a gas to measure its pressure.

 A thin filament (usually platinum or tungsten) is heated by electrical current inside a tube connected to the vacuum system.


 Gas molecules collide with the hot filament and carry heat away. At higher pressures, more heat is removed and the filament cools.

 At lower pressures, fewer molecules carry heat away and the filament stays hotter.


 The gauge circuit measures the filament resistance change. Since resistance changes with temperature, this gives a direct indication of gas molecule density, which is proportional to pressure.


 
 Pressure range
 Approximately 1000 Pa (1 atm) down to 0.1 Pa (10-3 mbar). Above 1000 Pa, all gauges at that pressure read similarly since gas conduction dominates. Below 0.1 Pa, the molecular mean free path exceeds the filament dimensions and thermal conductivity becomes pressure-independent.


 Accuracy
 Typical accuracy is 10 to 15% of reading within the useful range. Accuracy drops significantly above 10 mbar and below 0.01 mbar.


 Gas type effect
 The Pirani gauge is calibrated for air or nitrogen. Gases with different thermal conductivities (hydrogen, argon, helium) give incorrect readings unless a gas correction factor is applied. Hydrogen reads high (appears at lower pressure than actual). Argon reads low (appears at higher pressure than actual).


 Applications
 Roughing pump monitoring, vacuum oven control, leak detection setup, and pre-valve interlocking before high vacuum systems are opened to prevent contamination.





 Penning Gauge Working Principle


 The Penning gauge is a cold cathode ionisation gauge. It measures pressure by counting ions produced when electrons collide with gas molecules inside a strong magnetic field.


 A high voltage (2 to 4 kV) is applied between an anode ring and a cathode plate. A permanent magnet creates a field perpendicular to the electric field.

 Electrons from the cathode spiral in long helical paths along the magnetic field lines, greatly increasing the chance of ionising a gas molecule.


 The ion current from these collisions is measured by the gauge circuit. Higher current means more gas molecules and higher pressure.

 The relationship follows approximately I = k x P, where k is a gauge-specific constant.


 
 Pressure range
 10-2 to 10-7 mbar (1 to 10-5 Pa). Below 10-7 mbar, the ion current becomes too small to measure reliably. Above 10-2 mbar, the discharge becomes unstable and the reading is unreliable.


 Accuracy
 Typical accuracy is 20 to 50% of reading. The Penning gauge is not a precision instrument but is robust and reliable for vacuum system monitoring and interlock control.


 Gas type effect
 Like the Pirani gauge, the Penning gauge is gas-type dependent. The ionisation efficiency varies between gas species. Correction factors are applied for gases other than nitrogen. In processes using argon or reactive gases, the uncorrected reading can be 30 to 50% different from the actual pressure.


 Applications
 High vacuum monitoring in sputter deposition, electron beam equipment, and particle accelerators. Commonly used for interlock systems that prevent process tools from operating above a set vacuum level.





 Penning gauge contamination risk: The Penning gauge can become contaminated by process gases, oils, or vapours that coat the electrodes. A contaminated gauge gives a low pressure reading (appears better than actual) because the contamination reduces ion emission. Regularly degas the gauge by running it at elevated temperature, or replace the electrode insert if readings drift persistently in a known-clean system.
